claim: Starting March 1, 2026, VPC Encryption Controls moved from a free preview to a paid feature: a fixed hourly rate for every non-empty VPC (one with network interfaces) that has Encryption Controls on in monitor or enforce mode; empty VPCs with Encryption Controls on are not charged.
question: Since when is VPC Encryption Controls charged, what was it before, and which VPCs are billed?

values.spoken: it used to be a free preview

values.display: fixed hourly rate for every non-empty VPC
values.spoken: a fixed hourly rate for each VPC that has network interfaces

qualifiers.scope: per non-empty VPC, per hour, per Region
qualifiers.condition: Encryption Controls enabled in monitor or enforce mode

evidence.quote: Starting March 1, 2026, VPC Encryption Controls will transition from a free preview to a paid feature. You will be charged a fixed hourly rate for every non-empty VPC (VPC that has network interfaces in them) that has Encryption Controls enabled in either monitor or enforce mode. There will be no charge for empty VPCs that have encryption controls enabled.
You are charged a flat rate (based on region) per hour for every non-empty VPC (VPC that has a network interface in it) that is running Encryption Controls in either “monitor” or “enforce” mode.

note: Paid since 2026-03-01; the feature itself GA 2025-11-21 (examinable). One line in Changed recently at most.

claim: When you enable encryption support on a transit gateway, VPC Encryption Controls charges apply to every VPC attached to that transit gateway, whatever its Encryption Controls mode (monitor, enforce or off), even an empty VPC.
question: Does enabling encryption support on a transit gateway create VPC Encryption Controls charges for the attached VPCs?

values.display: standard VPC Encryption Controls charges apply to all VPCs attached to that Transit Gateway
values.spoken: every attached VPC is billed, even empty ones

qualifiers.scope: per VPC attached to a transit gateway with encryption support
qualifiers.condition: encryption support enabled on the transit gateway

evidence.quote: When you enable encryption support on a Transit Gateway, standard VPC Encryption Controls charges apply to all VPCs attached to that Transit Gateway irrespective of their encryption controls mode (monitor, enforce or off) even if they are empty.

note: Announced with the pricing post of March 1, 2026. Chapter 11 owns Transit Gateway; pointer only.

claim: Since November 11, 2022, three IPv6 addresses are reserved for the default VPC router: the subnet's ::1 address plus two link-local addresses (one in the FE80::/10 range and FE80:ec2::1).
question: Which IPv6 addresses does the default VPC router use, and when did that change?

values.display: Three IPv6 addresses are now reserved for use by the default VPC router

evidence.quote: | [IPv6 default gateway router configuration](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/configure-subnets.html#subnet-sizing) | Three IPv6 addresses are now reserved for use by the default VPC router. | November 11, 2022 |
In addition to the IP address reserved by AWS for the VPC router in the example above, the following IPv6 addresses are reserved for the default VPC router:
A link-local IPv6 address in the FE80::/10 range generated using EUI-64.
`2001:db8:1234:1a00::1`: Reserved by AWS for the VPC router.

note: Does not change the count of unusable addresses in an IPv6 subnet (first four and last, see vpc-subnet-ipv6-five-reserved); the two extra router addresses are link-local. FE80:ec2::1 is quoted on the same page.

claim: Since October 4, 2022 you can enable Network Address Usage (NAU) metrics for a VPC; NAU is a metric applied to resources in the VPC that helps you plan for and monitor the size of the VPC.
question: What is Network Address Usage and when did the metric arrive?

values.display: plan for and monitor the size of your VPC
values.spoken: a size metric for a VPC

evidence.quote: | [Network Address Usage metrics](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/network-address-usage.html) | You can enable Network Address Usage metrics for your VPC to help you plan for and monitor the size of your VPC. | October 4, 2022 |
Network Address Usage (NAU) is a metric applied to resources in your virtual network to help you plan for and monitor the size of your VPC.

note: The NAU quotas (64,000 per VPC, 128,000 peered) are separate quota facts.

claim: Since August 13, 2025 an internet gateway can route inbound traffic for a large pool of public IP addresses (for example a BYOIP pool) to a single network interface; previously it only accepted traffic for public IP addresses directly associated with network interfaces in the VPC.
question: Can an internet gateway route inbound traffic for a whole public IP pool to one network interface, and since when?

values.display: route inbound internet traffic destined for large pools of public IP addresses to a single elastic network interface
values.spoken: a whole public IP pool to one network interface

evidence.quote: You can route inbound internet traffic destined for large pools of public IP addresses to a single elastic network interface (ENI) in your VPC.
Previously, internet gateways only accepted traffic destined for public IP addresses that were directly associated with network interfaces in the VPC.

| [Route inbound VPC traffic to public IP addresses](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/igw-ingress-routing.html) | You can now configure advanced routing rules to direct inbound traffic from the internet to specific public IP addresses within your VPC, enabling more granular control over traffic flow and routing decisions for ingress scenarios. | August 13, 2025 |

changed.was: only accepted traffic destined for public IP addresses that were directly associated with network interfaces in the VPC

note: Telco and IoT niche; at most a name-level mention. The change feed also lists 'Amazon VPC now supports IPv4 ingress routing for large IP Pools' on 2025-08-15.

claim: Public IP Insights, a feature of Amazon VPC IP Address Manager (IPAM) available at no cost, helps you monitor, analyze and audit your use of public IPv4 addresses; it launched with the announcement of the public IPv4 charge.
question: Which tool helps you find and audit the public IPv4 addresses you pay for?

values.spoken: Public IP Insights in VPC IPAM, free

evidence.quote: In order to make it easier for you to monitor, analyze, and audit your use of public IPv4 addresses, today we are launching Public IP Insights, a new feature of Amazon VPC IP Address Manager that is available to you at no cost.

note: Launched July 28, 2023 per the change feed.

claim: To reduce the public IPv4 charge, AWS points to Elastic Load Balancers for inbound traffic and NAT gateways for outbound traffic instead of a public IPv4 address on each instance, and to faster adoption of IPv6.
question: How can a workload avoid paying for a public IPv4 address on every instance?

values.display: use Elastic Load Balancers and NAT Gateways for ingress and egress traffic
values.spoken: load balancer in, NAT gateway out, no public IP per instance

evidence.quote: A new blog post shows you how to use Elastic Load Balancers and NAT Gateways for ingress and egress traffic, while avoiding the use of a public IPv4 address for each instance that you launch.

This change reflects our own costs and is also intended to encourage you to be a bit more frugal with your use of public IPv4 addresses and to think about accelerating your adoption of IPv6 as a modernization and conservation measure.

note: Best-answer shift from FRESHNESS: cost answers now favor IPv6, or a NAT gateway or load balancer front end.

claim: EC2 Instance Connect can connect to instances using their private IPv4 addresses, so you no longer need public IPv4 addresses for administrative access (generally SSH or RDP).
question: Do you need a public IPv4 address on an instance for SSH or RDP administration?

values.display: you no longer need to use public IPv4 addresses for administrative purposes
values.spoken: no public IP needed for admin access

evidence.quote: Earlier this year we enhanced EC2 Instance Connect and gave it the ability to connect to your instances using private IPv4 addresses. As a result, you no longer need to use public IPv4 addresses for administrative purposes (generally using SSH or RDP).

note: The book teaches Session Manager first (chapter 38); this fact supports the 'no public IP for admin access' point. Chapter 13 (EC2) may own the EC2 Instance Connect Endpoint detail.

claim: Even before February 1, 2024, an idle Elastic IP address in the account and an additional (secondary) Elastic IP address on a running EC2 instance were charged at $0.005 per IP per hour; the 2024 change added the charge for in-use public IPv4 addresses.
question: Which public IPv4 addresses were already charged before February 2024, and which became charged?

evidence.quote: | Idle Elastic IP Address in account | $0.005 | $0.005 |
evidence.table_header: | Public IP Address Type | Current Price/Hour (USD) | New Price/Hour (USD) (Effective February 1, 2024) |

evidence.quote: | Additional (secondary) Elastic IP Address on a running EC2 instance | $0.005 | $0.005 |
evidence.table_header: | Public IP Address Type | Current Price/Hour (USD) | New Price/Hour (USD) (Effective February 1, 2024) |

evidence.quote: We are introducing a new charge for public IPv4 addresses. Effective February 1, 2024 there will be a charge of $0.005 per IP per hour for all public IPv4 addresses, whether attached to a service or not (there is already a charge for public IPv4 addresses you allocate in your account but don’t attach to an EC2 instance).

note: Older questions that say 'an idle Elastic IP costs money but an attached one is free' were right before 2024-02-01; only the second half changed.
